clinical_knowledge.topic: Squamous Cell Carcinoma scalp evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Squamous Cell Carcinoma scalp is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes biopsy confirmation followed by wide local excision with margins, recognizing that SCC arising in a chronic burn scar (Marjolin ulcer) behaves more aggressively and carries higher metastatic risk than typical sun-related SCC, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: non-healing scaly bleeding red patch on scalp
Key HPI features: A 23-year-old male presents with a non-healing, scaly, bleeding red patch that developed within an old childhood scalp burn scar, gradually enlarging over the past several months.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Ulcerated, indurated, scaly plaque with rolled, everted edges arising within a hypopigmented burn scar on the scalp; friable with bleeding on contact. No overlying hair growth within the lesion. Palpation of cervical/occipital lymph nodes for regional spread.
Relevant background/PMH: Childhood scalp burn injury (age 8) treated with skin grafting, with the graft/scar site now showing malignant-appearing changes
common_misconceptions: Assuming SCC only arises from chronic sun damage in older patients and missing SCC arising in a chronic wound or burn scar (Marjolin ulcer) in a younger patient.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Flap ischemia or tissue necrosis.
management_principles: SCC arising in a chronic wound/scar (Marjolin ulcer) is rare but should be suspected in a non-healing lesion within an old burn scar, even in a young patient
Confirm the diagnosis with a full-thickness (punch or incisional) biopsy sampling the ulcer edge and base

Perform wide local excision with margins wider than typical sun-related SCC given the more aggressive behavior and higher metastatic potential of Marjolin ulcer, with nodal staging/imaging if there is palpable lymphadenopathy or high-risk features
Refer to plastic surgery for excision and reconstruction planning, and arrange long-term surveillance given the elevated recurrence and metastasis risk.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: A 23-year-old male presents with a non-healing, scaly, bleeding red patch that developed within an old childhood scalp burn scar, gradually enlarging over the past several months.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Ulcerated, indurated, scaly plaque with rolled, everted edges arising within a hypopigmented burn scar on the scalp; friable with bleeding on contact. No overlying hair growth within the lesion. No palpable cervical/occipital lymphadenopathy.
reference_soap.assessment: Non-healing ulcerated plaque within a chronic burn scar, highly suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma arising in the scar (Marjolin ulcer), pending biopsy confirmation.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm with a full-thickness biopsy of the ulcer edge and base. If confirmed, perform wide local excision with margins wider than typical sun-related SCC given the more aggressive behavior of Marjolin ulcer, with nodal staging if lymphadenopathy is present. Refer to plastic surgery for excision and reconstruction planning, and arrange long-term surveillance.
